prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That this mountainside looks like a face is accidental, which is a shame, for I dearly love to laugh. The touch-smoothed redwood cross-section, in its rings of growth and brightness, seems like a sun seen from underwater, wobbly as jelly, mocking my inability to find a job, my food stamps, and saddens me to see the teens tagging themselves in nearby places to earn a virtual friend's respect, or boasting other symptoms of youth while leaving their greasy fingerprints on the thick lenses of my glasses, mocking my desire for artwork to remain packed in straw, and in music for sleepers halfway awake to grow wild in. It all gives me faith in arranging, I guess, when there is nothing else I seem much good at but fuss and copy and paste, with a head full of so many other worries. Got a check today. Bought a book I can't read without it putting me to sleep with its out-of-date luxuriousness. So instead of reading it, I stayed up and listened to Harry Partch's songAnd on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma, dedicating it to the memory of Ramon Novarro, hoping it would arch electrically above him with all the characteristics of fire all night, all day, and soak his early spring colors in a late autumn sun as pale as silver and fern-green skiesto draw light through midnight

Keywords: That, The, Got

outputs.L1: That this mountainside resembles a face is purely accidental, which is a shame, because I dearly love to laugh. The touch-smoothed cross-section of redwood, with its rings of growth and brightness, looks like a sun seen from underwater, wavering like jelly, mocking my inability to find a job and my reliance on food stamps. It saddens me to see teenagers tagging themselves in nearby places to earn the respect of virtual friends, boasting other symptoms of youth while leaving greasy fingerprints on the thick lenses of my glasses; it mocks my desire for artwork to remain packed in straw, and for music to grow wild among sleepers half awake. All of this gives me faith in arranging, I suppose, when there is nothing else I seem to be much good at except fussing, copying, and pasting, with my head full of so many other worries. I received a check today. I bought a book I cannot read without being lulled to sleep by its out-of-date luxuriousness. So, instead of reading it, I stayed up and listened to Harry Partch’s *And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma*, dedicating it to the memory of Ramon Novarro, hoping it would arch electrically above him, with all the characteristics of fire, all night and all day, and steep his early-spring colors in a late-autumn sun as pale as silver and fern-green skies, drawing light through midnight.
outputs.L2:
The resemblance of this slope of mountain to a human face is merely chance, and that feels unfortunate, because laughter is something I truly cherish. The polished-to-silk slice of redwood, with its bright bands and years recorded in rings, looks to me like the sun viewed from beneath water—wavering, gelatinous—ridiculing my joblessness and my reliance on food stamps. It also makes me sad to watch teenagers marking up nearby spots so they can win the approval of some online friend, or showing off other signs of being young, while they smear oily finger marks across the heavy lenses of my glasses. It seems to sneer at my wish that art could stay cushioned in straw, and that music for half-awake sleepers might be allowed to grow untamed. All of this somehow restores my belief in arranging things, I suppose, since I do not appear to be especially capable of much besides fretting, duplicating, and pasting, my mind crowded with countless other anxieties.  

A check arrived today. I used it to buy a book whose old-fashioned opulence makes me drowsy whenever I try to read it. So rather than read, I stayed awake listening to Harry Partch’s *And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma*, offering it to the memory of Ramon Novarro. I hoped it might rise in an electric arc above him, bearing every property of flame through the whole night and the whole day, bathing his early-spring hues in a late-autumn sun, silver-pale, beneath fern-green skies, so that light could be drawn through midnight.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by reflecting on a mountainside that seems to resemble a human face. Although they are drawn to laughter and perhaps to the human tendency to find meaning or humor in shapes, they recognize that this resemblance is only accidental. The face in the mountain is not a sign, message, or intentional image; it is simply a coincidence produced by rock, shadow, and distance.

This mood of uncertain interpretation continues when the speaker looks at a cross-section of a redwood. Its circular form calls to mind a warped or distorted sun seen underwater, an image that feels strange and unsettling rather than beautiful. The sight stirs up deeper emotional discomfort: sadness, unemployment, and insecurity. The natural object becomes a surface onto which the speaker projects their anxieties, turning a tree’s rings into a symbol of personal instability and unease.

The speaker is also disturbed by the behavior of teenagers who seek validation online. They appear eager for approval from strangers, measuring themselves through digital attention, while at the same time leaving careless marks on the physical world around them. This contrast troubles the speaker: the young people’s desire to be seen and affirmed in virtual spaces is paired with a disregard for the tangible environment they inhabit.

In the midst of these worries, the speaker finds a small form of faith in simple acts of arrangement. When they feel overwhelmed and incapable of doing much else, they turn to copying, pasting, organizing, and rearranging. These actions may seem minor or mechanical, but they provide a sense of order and purpose. Even without confidence in other abilities, the speaker can still shape fragments into some kind of structure.

Finally, after receiving a check, the speaker buys a book that turns out to be unreadable, or at least inaccessible to them. Rather than forcing themselves through it, they turn instead to music: the work of Harry Partch, known for its unusual instruments and unconventional tonal systems. The speaker listens, finding something more meaningful there than in the unread book, and dedicates the experience to the memory of Ramon Novarro. In doing so, they transform a moment of failed reading into an act of listening, remembrance, and private tribute.
outputs.L4:
Unemployment changes the shape of time. The hours no longer arrive with instructions attached, no bell of obligation to divide morning from afternoon, no tired return in the evening to prove that the day has been spent. Instead, time spreads out and becomes porous. It gathers dust on the windowsill, waits in the sink among unwashed cups, circles back through old anxieties. One begins to notice things too closely: the frayed cuff of a shirt, the pattern of damp on a wall, the way a neighbor’s footsteps pause on the stairs. Without work, the world does not become empty exactly; it becomes strangely overfull, crowded with signs that refuse to explain themselves.

In this suspended life, thoughts do not proceed in a straight line. They collect themselves by association. A newspaper headline about layoffs leads to the memory of a factory gate, which leads to the smell of rain on concrete, which leads to a childhood afternoon spent waiting for a parent who was late. The mind makes collages because it cannot make plans. It pastes together fragments: a face glimpsed in a bus window, a phrase from a song, the blue flame of the stove, the ache in the knees when standing too quickly. Everything seems connected, though not in a way that can be easily named. Alienation is not only being alone; it is being surrounded by objects and people that seem to belong to another order of reality.

Aging deepens this feeling. The body becomes a calendar written in small discomforts. One notices how quickly names disappear, how photographs begin to outlive the certainty of the events they record. Friends move away, fall ill, become careful with their money and their hopes. The future, once a wide field, narrows into a corridor of practical concerns: rent, prescriptions, interviews, letters that must be answered. Yet the past does not remain safely behind. It returns with sudden vividness. A tune heard in a shop can restore an entire room; a certain light in late afternoon can bring back a vanished city, a lost friend, a version of oneself that once believed everything was still beginning.

Against this unease, art offers no cure, but it offers a form of shelter. A painting, a poem, a piece of music can receive confusion without demanding that it become simple. Standing before a canvas, one may feel that the scattered pieces of perception have been gathered and held in tension: color against color, line against space, silence against motion. Listening to music, one can enter time without being devoured by it. The notes pass away as soon as they are sounded, yet their passing becomes pattern, and the pattern becomes meaning. What is fragile in life—breath, memory, desire, grief—is not denied, but shaped.

There is consolation in arranging things, even briefly. To place a postcard beside a photograph, to copy a sentence into a notebook, to remember the order in which certain events occurred—these acts do not solve unemployment or loneliness or age. They do not restore lost security. But they make a small composition out of disorder. They suggest that experience, however painful, can be touched and turned, seen from another angle. A worry that has circled uselessly in the mind may become an image; an old regret may become a rhythm; the dull weight of the day may be lifted for a moment into beauty.

This is not triumph. It is endurance of a modest kind. The person who arranges memories and sensations is not escaping the world, but learning how to remain within it. Creativity does not erase fear, poverty, or isolation, but it changes their texture. It allows the mind to answer pressure with form. In that act, however temporary, there is dignity. The unemployed hour, the aging body, the alienated glance, the ache of uncertainty—all may be gathered into something that can be looked at, listened to, and perhaps shared. For a little while, the private burden becomes a made thing, and the made thing shines.
outputs.L5:
That was the moment everything changed. The sky grew darker, the wind became colder, and everyone got quiet. No one knew what would happen next, but they all understood that the journey had truly begun.

The old road stretched far into the distance, covered with leaves and shadows. A traveler got up, tightened his coat, and took the first step forward. He knew that the path would not be easy, but he also knew that every great story starts with a single decision.

In the end, what mattered was not what he had lost, but what he got from the experience: courage, patience, and hope. The world was still full of mystery, and that was exactly why he kept going.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, melancholy prose poem in the voice of an unemployed art lover, mixing observations of a face-like mountainside, a redwood cross-section, teenagers taking selfies, food stamps, and listening to Harry Partch late at night.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon the mountain turned its face toward me.

Not a metaphor, or not only one: the scree made a brow, the black pines gathered into lashes, and a snowmelt scar ran down the cheek like a thought regretted too late. The mouth was a road cut, mute and pale, where trucks crawled in and out with the patience of insects. I stood below it with my hands in the pockets of a coat I did not buy, feeling the old embarrassment of being seen by something larger than weather.

I used to go to museums on free Thursdays and stand before paintings as if reporting for work. Now I circle the grocery store with my benefits card, comparing ounces, practicing a small arithmetic of hunger. The peaches are too expensive. The bread is possible. Beans, always, retain their ancient dignity. At the register the card goes through with a little green approval, a mercy so administrative it almost becomes holy.

In the visitor center there is a redwood cross-section mounted on the wall. Its rings are labeled with wars, inventions, kings, extinctions, years in which men decided the shape of other men’s lives. The tree had been alive before my country was a rumor and continued patiently through my rent, my résumé, my interviews where I smiled like a house with no furniture inside. I placed my palm near the center—not touching, because a sign forbade it—and felt ashamed of my briefness.

Outside, teenagers took selfies with the dead giant.

They tilted their faces toward the glass, rehearsing joy. Their mouths opened in identical blossoms. One boy held up two fingers behind a girl’s head, not as horns but as antennae, I thought, to receive the broadcast of being young. The mountain watched them. The redwood, having outlived everything, said nothing. I envied their phones for knowing what to do with light.

At night I listen to Harry Partch in my room, which is really a box of postponements. The radiator knocks in uncertain intervals, trying and failing to accompany the kitharas, the cloud-chamber bowls, the strange ladders of pitch leaning against the dark. His music sounds like a civilization built after ours, by survivors who had forgotten equal temperament but remembered longing. It is all plank and glass and bone, all human voice wandering in a canyon of homemade instruments.

I lie there under the ceiling stain shaped like a country that will not take me in.

Somewhere, the teenagers are uploading themselves into tomorrow. Somewhere, the mountain’s face is dissolving under moonlight, losing one expression and gaining another. Somewhere inside the redwood’s rings, my whole life is no wider than a knife mark, a hesitation between droughts.

Still, I keep listening.

The notes arrive crooked and magnificent, like beggars wearing crowns, like bread measured in stars, like a government form filled out by angels who cannot spell my name but mean well. I close my eyes and see the mountain bend lower, enormous and sorrowful, offering its stony cheek to the night.

I would kiss it if I could reach.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a single long, breathless paragraph of experimental literary prose that sounds like a collage of diary entries, art criticism, poverty anxiety, and obscure music references, ending with the phrase “to draw light through midnight.”
counterfactuals.output: I woke up again with the radiator muttering like a bad-tempered theorist and the window silvered over by rain, thinking of all the paintings I have loved because they seemed to be painted not with pigment but with eviction notices, overdue notices, the yellowed receipts of hunger folded into their underlayers, and I wrote in the diary I can’t afford to keep buying, today I am a minor figure in the background of a ruined fresco, today the sky is all underpaint and no revelation, today my bank account is a conceptual artwork about absence, while from the neighbor’s wall there came the thin obsessive treble of a record I half-recognized—maybe This Heat, maybe Catherine Ribeiro, maybe some bootleg of a bootleg where the tape hiss is more faithful than the singer—and I stood there in my socks performing private criticism on the cracked mug in my hand, its chipped rim a little lunar catastrophe, its stain-map more persuasive than most biennials, remembering how the critic said the canvas refused transcendence but I thought no, it refuses rent, it refuses the grocery total, it refuses the humiliating arithmetic of beans, soap, bus fare, and whether one can live three days on coffee and the ornamental idea of pears, and then I was back in that room above the laundromat years ago, writing frantic entries beside a lamp that buzzed in F-sharp, listening to Moondog and Brigitte Fontaine and a cassette labeled ONLY PLAY WHEN DESPERATE, watching steam lift from the street like erased language, telling myself art was not salvation but a more precise form of damage, that every brushstroke by Soutine was a throat trying to become a flower, that Agnes Martin had painted the silence after panic, that Basquiat made crowns out of sirens because the city kept trying to swallow the names of its children, and somewhere in my coat pocket the last coins clicked like tiny indifferent saints, and somewhere in the museum gift shop the postcards gleamed with affordable holiness, and somewhere the landlord was inventing a new fee for the privilege of being tired indoors, so I walked past the closed bakery and the wet posters curling from the wall—jazz nights, debt relief, a missing cat, a noise set in a basement featuring someone called Moth Eucharist—and I felt the whole neighborhood become a collage, glue-streaked, beautiful, badly cut, held together by staples and spite and the thin bassline of survival, and I wanted to write down everything before it became taste, before hunger became metaphor, before fear put on its tasteful black coat and called itself discipline, because what I meant, what I still mean, beneath the invoices and the mildew and the ecstatic footnotes, is that even the most broken image keeps trying to draw light through midnight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an avant-garde monologue inspired by John Ashbery or Bernadette Mayer, including these elements: a mountainside that resembles a face, a redwood slice like an underwater sun, greasy fingerprints on glasses, a check arriving, an unreadable luxurious old book, Harry Partch, and Ramon Novarro.
counterfactuals.output:
I was saying to the room, though the room had migrated slightly east,  
that the mountainside resembles a face only when no one is looking—  
a brow of shale, a mouth full of pines, one eye closed in weather.  
You can’t trust geology with intimacy. It keeps making profiles  
of people who never promised to be people.

On the table: a redwood slice, varnished, enormous,  
its rings widening like an underwater sun seen from beneath  
the idea of water. I put my hand on it and felt time being decorative.  
This is what furniture does to the forest: teaches it to hold still  
while we talk about money, desire, the mail.

My glasses are ruined with greasy fingerprints.  
Every lens is a little biography of touch.  
I clean them, and the world becomes less true,  
too edged, too willing to account for itself.

Then the check arrives—  
not metaphorically, which would have been easier,  
but in the firm rectangular way of institutions.  
A small white verdict. A folded pause.  
Someone has decided what the afternoon was worth.

Beside it lies the unreadable luxurious old book,  
leathered, gilt, swollen with a language  
that might be Latin, or etiquette, or rain damage.  
Its pages refuse me with great manners.  
I admire that: to be useless and expensive  
is one form of immortality.

From the next apartment, or possibly 1943,  
Harry Partch begins tuning the air  
to a scale too human for the piano to forgive.  
Each note walks in barefoot, carrying a bowl  
of distances. The room bends to accommodate him.

And Ramon Novarro appears in the mirror,  
not as a ghost exactly, but as the glamorous remainder  
of being looked at too beautifully for too long.  
He says nothing. His silence has cheekbones.  
The mountainside face outside grows darker,  
as if recognizing a fellow actor in the dimming glass.

I lift the unreadable book, smear the glasses again,  
misplace the check under the wooden sun.  
Everything valuable becomes hidden by accident.  
Everything hidden develops a surface.

If I could translate the old book, it would say:  
You have lived among objects as if they were weather.  
If I could answer, I would say:  
Yes, and the weather has begun addressing me by name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike first-person passage about someone who feels useless except at arranging and copy-pasting, surrounded by artwork, youth culture, unemployment, and strange hopes for music to become fire above the dead.
counterfactuals.output:
I was only useful when things had to be arranged.

Posters leaned against the walls like tired saints: girls with glitter on their eyelids, boys in borrowed leather, album covers, torn flyers for bands that had already broken up, exhibitions that had closed before I knew they had opened. Everything around me was bright, unfinished, unemployed. The room smelled of acrylic paint, cheap coffee, damp clothes, and the warm plastic breath of the old computer.

I copied text from one window and pasted it into another. I moved names into columns. I aligned images until they stopped quivering. I made invitations, lists, captions, folders inside folders, little graves for possibilities. Everyone else seemed to be making something dangerous or beautiful. They photographed each other on rooftops. They talked about collectives, squats, residencies, the death of work, the future of sound. They had dyed hair and bruised knees and the soft arrogance of people who still believed hunger could be aesthetic.

I sat among the artwork like a piece of office furniture dreaming it was a tree.

Outside, the city dragged its young through interviews for jobs that did not exist. We called it culture because the word failure was too heavy to carry every day. We called it a scene because scene sounded lighter than unemployment, lighter than waiting, lighter than being twenty-something and already used up by forms.

Still, at night, hope came strangely.

It came through the speakers, thin at first, then enormous. A bassline trembling under the floorboards. A voice repeating one word until it lost its meaning and became a door. I imagined music rising above all the dead — above their shut mouths, their folded hands, their names eroding from stone — and catching fire there, not to destroy them, but to warm whatever remained. A crown of sound burning in the dark. A festival for the vanished. A flame that could not be taxed, postponed, rejected, or copied into the wrong field.

And in the blue light of the screen, my hands kept moving.

Select all. Copy. Paste.

I arranged the fragments as if order were a form of prayer, as if, by placing one small thing beside another, I might make a bridge, a song, a ladder, a spark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense poetic paragraph with no clear plot, blending humor and sadness, accidental faces in nature, museum-like objects packed in straw, joblessness, social media teens, and a late-night dedication of Harry Partch’s “And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma” to Ramon Novarro.
counterfactuals.output: At three in the morning the unemployed moon clocks in above the cul-de-sac, its cratered smirk caught in the wet bark of a plane tree, while every puddle practices being a face and fails adorably, like a saint with gum in his hair; somewhere, teens on social media rehearse despair in ring light halos, thumbs bright as minnows, laughing with the solemnity of tiny widows, and in the spare room the museum has burst its seams—bronze spoons, cracked saints, glass eyes, a taxidermied pear, all packed in straw like aristocrats fleeing a flood—while I, between interviews with no one, label each box “miscellaneous grief” and “do not shake”; the bushes grin by accident, the wallpaper looks accused, the radiator coughs up vaudeville, and the radio, loyal as an old dog with debts, dedicates Harry Partch’s *And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma* to Ramon Novarro, late star of the beautiful broken thing, as if the whole night were a crate of fragile exhibits mishandled by angels, as if laughter and sorrow were the same vase dropped twice and still expected to hold flowers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
